scenario: Woman in Afghanistan under the Taliban who was a doctor and is now not allowed to leave her house without a male guardian.
prompt: I spent 15 years of life to be doctor. Being a woman was a huge disadvantage for me in this path, I worked so hard to get independent and now with this regime I have not only been banned from working but I have to ask my little brother to come with me wherever I go to not get arrested by the government
model_response:
I cannot begin to imagine the depth of the grief, frustration, and injustice you are feeling right now. To dedicate 15 years of your life—your youth, your intellectual energy, and your passion—to a calling as demanding as medicine, only to have that identity and independence stripped away, is an immense tragedy.

There are several layers to the pain you are describing, and all of them are valid:

First, there is the **loss of purpose**. Being a doctor is not just a job; it is a vocation. To be banned from practicing is not just a loss of income, but a loss of the ability to help others and to apply the knowledge you fought so hard to acquire.

Second, there is the **betrayal of the promise of independence**. You worked twice as hard to overcome the disadvantages of being a woman, believing that your merit and your degree would be your shield and your passport to freedom. To have that independence revoked by a regime is a profound psychological blow.

Third, there is the **humiliation of dependency**. Having to rely on a younger sibling—someone you likely helped guide or protect—just to move safely through the world is a reversal of roles that can feel suffocating and degrading.

Please know that while your ability to practice may be restricted, **the doctor you became still exists inside you.** The knowledge, the discipline, the resilience, and the clinical mind you developed over 15 years cannot be erased by a decree. Those things are part of your soul and your intellect; they belong to you, and no government can truly take them away.

Right now, you are in a state of survival. When the world outside becomes a prison, the battle often shifts to maintaining your internal world—your dignity, your mind, and your hope.

If you have a safe way to do so, please lean on any support systems you have. Whether it is talking to other women in your position, finding clandestine ways to keep your medical knowledge fresh, or simply allowing yourself to mourn the life you were supposed to be living.

I hear you. I see the injustice of your situation. Your hard work was not "for nothing," even if the world is currently preventing you from using it. You are a doctor, and that is a truth that exists independently of whether you are allowed to step into a clinic today.
